dcf._betaWhy: No bank debt and net cash, so the 12.2% cost of equity is the discount rate; beta 0.95, as for IHCL and ITC Hotels: travel demand is cyclical (Covid, the 2026 West Asia shock), no financial leverage.
dcf._tgWhy: Indian luxury travel grows with nominal GDP; 6% nominal, the top of the house range (IHCL, ITC Hotels).
dcf._fadeGrowthWhy: Revenue growth fades from ~12% to 8% by year 15 as the owned pipeline opens and rate growth normalises.
dcf._fadeMarginWhy: 36%: near FY29E; EIH earned 37-38% in FY24-25 before the flight-catering mix shift.
dcf._fadeCapexWhy: Capex fades from ~20% of revenue (FY29E, Hebbal and the owned pipeline) to 12%: EIH grows mainly by owning (825 owned keys in the pipeline vs 1,833 managed), renovation ~5% plus growth keys.

bull.label: Bull
bull.narrative: Foreign arrivals return by H2FY27, owned RevPAR grows ~14-15% a year, Rajgarh and the Grand ramp fast, EIH keeps Wildflower Hall on a long contract and the market pays the top quartile of EIH's own post-Covid multiple range after the same sector move.

bear.label: Bear
bear.narrative: The 2026 travel shock lingers (Oberoi hotels depend more on foreign guests), RevPAR grows ~6-7%, Wildflower Hall is lost, project delays (Grand, Gandikota, Goa) continue, labour-code wage costs stick and the multiple stays at the bottom quartile after the sector de-rating.

cover.headline: The best hotels in India at a multiple that looks cheap, until you see the whole sector fell and the next new rooms are three years away
cover.lead: EIH owns and runs the Oberoi and Trident hotels (3,801 keys in India, 408 abroad), flight kitchens and a 36.81% stake in listed EIH Associated Hotels; Reliance (18.8%) and ITC (16.1%) sit beside the Oberoi family (32.9%). Q1FY27 revenue rose 14.5% and owned-hotel RevPAR 14%, but operating EBITDA only 4% (Rajgarh ramp-up, renovations, labour-code wages). Coverage is thin: Axis Capital initiated with Buy at ₹385 on 29-Sep-26; hotel stocks are valued on **EV/EBITDA**. EIH trades at 14.1x one-year-forward EV/EBITDA, below its post-Covid median of 15.9x, but its three usable listed peers (IHCL −17%, ITC Hotels −20%, Lemon Tree −39%) had de-rated by a median −20% by 30-Sep-2026. The house rule gives **13x Sep-28E EBITDA** and a sum of the parts of **{{dcf.tp|inr}} ({{dcf.upside|chg}}): we initiate with HOLD.** We forecast EBITDA of ₹1,150 / 1,305 / 1,494 cr and EPS of ₹13.2 / 14.8 / 16.9 (FY27-29E). Cross-checks are lower (P/E ₹269, DCF ₹227). Bull {{scen.bull.tp|inr}}; bear {{scen.bear.tp|inr}}.

arguments.p: In FY26 Oberoi hotels earned RevPAR of ₹22,004 (+10%), 1.9x India's luxury-segment average; 14 of 15 benchmarked hotels rank first or second in their markets and owned-hotel occupancy was 76.8%. No other listed Indian hotel company has this concentration of top-end assets.

arguments.h: But growth has stalled and will stay rate-led until FY29
arguments.p: Revenue grew 9% in FY25 and 7% in FY26 with almost no new rooms; the Grand Kolkata (209 keys) and Trident Jaipur are shut for renovation, Wildflower Hall is run on an interim contract, and the 825 owned pipeline keys open mostly in 2028-30. We model revenue +{{F.salesGrowth.0|pct}} / +{{F.salesGrowth.1|pct}} / +{{F.salesGrowth.2|pct}} and EPS growth of ~14% a year (FY26-29E, before one-offs).

arguments.h: Rich balance sheet, governance to watch
arguments.p: No bank debt, ~₹1,340 cr of net cash after leases, CARE AA+. Against that: a reported family dispute over the promoter holding, the two executive Oberois paid ~₹16 cr each (465-470x the median employee), a royalty to a promoter company, a ₹30 cr political donation in FY26, and exceptional items in five of the last six years.

arguments.h: Valuation: cheaper than its history, as is the sector
arguments.p: At ₹301 the market pays ~12.3x Sep-28E EBITDA once the other parts are valued our way; our derived multiple is 13x. Axis's ₹385 needs ~16.2x, close to EIH's own median with no sector adjustment. The DCF needs a ~10.8% discount rate to justify the price, below our 12.2%. We would buy below ~₹275.

catalysts: Q2FY27 results (due by mid-November 2026): renovations end in Q2; management said Q2 business on books was "very positive" and expected foreign guests to stay weak until Q3.

Wildflower Hall: the Himachal government's auction for a long-term operator (EIH bid; qualifying bids were due 10-Sep-2026, a live auction follows). Winning on acceptable terms removes a risk; losing removes one of the group's best resorts.
Peak season (Oct-Mar): foreign arrivals after the West Asia conflict, BRICS 2026 and Aero India events in Delhi and Bengaluru, Rajgarh's first full winter.
Project milestones: Trident Visakhapatnam (associate, 2027), The Oberoi Grand reopening (~Sep-2028), Goa, London, Tirupati, Hebbal; any new owned or managed signings.
The promoter family dispute and any change in Reliance's or ITC's holdings.

sections.title: A luxury hotel owner first: Oberoi and Trident hotels it owns, a few it manages, flight kitchens on the side

blocks.p: EIH makes money mainly by **owning and running its own hotels**: it keeps all their revenue and costs. The Oberoi brand covers 14 luxury hotels and resorts in India (The Oberoi, Mumbai (237), The Oberoi, New Delhi (220), The Oberoi Grand, Kolkata (209), The Oberoi, Gurgaon (202), The Oberoi, Bengaluru (160) and the Vilas resorts in Agra, Udaipur, Jaipur, Ranthambhore, Chandigarh and Bandhavgarh) plus 6 hotels and cruisers abroad (Egypt, Morocco, Bali, Lombok, Mauritius). Trident is the five-star brand (Trident, Nariman Point (586), Trident, Bandra Kurla (439), Trident, Hyderabad (323) and others). Some Tridents (including Trident Jaipur and the Visakhapatnam project) are owned by **EIH Associated Hotels**, a listed associate (EIH 36.81%) that EIH manages; a few hotels are **managed for third parties** for a fee (management fees are not disclosed). Side businesses: **Oberoi Flight Services** (airline catering in Mumbai, Delhi, Chennai and Kolkata; ₹154 cr of revenue in Q1FY27), airport services, project management, and a 40% car-rental JV with Avis.

In FY26 consolidated revenue of ₹2,940 cr was rooms ₹1,411 cr (48%), food and beverage incl. flight catering ₹1,096 cr (37%) and other services ₹434 cr (15%). Owned hotels ran at 76.8% occupancy with RevPAR of ~₹17,400 (+8.5%). EIH reports a single segment, so the split of profit between hotels, flight catering and the international hotels is not disclosed.

sections.title: Demand ahead of supply for a fourth year, luxury rates still rising; the 2026 travel shock hit foreign guests and the sector's valuation

blocks.p: Branded supply in India's key hotel markets grows ~5% a year while demand grows faster, which has let hotels push rates for four years. FY26 industry occupancy was 67-69% with average rates Rs10,000-10,200 (+6-8%) and RevPAR +5-7% (HVS Anarock), despite the May-2025 conflict, a long monsoon, December flight disruptions and the West Asia war. Q1FY27 was better: occupancy 64-66% (+2-4 pp), rates Rs8,100-8,300 (+6-8%), RevPAR +11-13%, led by domestic demand while foreign arrivals at EIH fell ~10%. ICRA (29-Sep-2026) expects premium-hotel revenue to grow 7-9% in FY27 after 11% in FY26, with occupancy 72-74%. At the very top end the MD & CEO argues India is still "significantly underpriced" against Europe, North America and much of Asia, where $1,000+ room rates are normal.

blocks.p: Wildflower Hall (85 keys, Shimla) was owned by Mashobra Resort Ltd, a 1995 JV with the Himachal Pradesh government. blocks.callout: **Honest verdict:** EIH has a genuine moat in its product: guests pay the highest rates in India for Oberoi hotels and the hotels earn them back in occupancy. That moat protects margins, not growth. Without a large managed pipeline or many new owned hotels, the moat earns a premium return on a fixed set of rooms, and travel shocks (Covid, 2026) pass straight through.

sections.title: Revenue 1.8x pre-Covid and margins up from ~20% to ~35%; but growth slowed to 7-9% in FY25-26 and margins slipped

blocks.p: Consolidated revenue was ₹1,596 cr in FY20, collapsed to ₹494 cr in FY21 (Covid) and reached ₹2,940 cr in FY26. The rebound was fast (FY23 ₹2,019 cr, FY24 ₹2,511 cr, +24%) and then slowed to +9% in FY25 and +7% in FY26, because EIH added almost no rooms: The Oberoi Grand Kolkata (209 keys) and Trident Jaipur (132 keys) closed for renovation, Wildflower Hall passed to the Himachal government, and only Rajgarh (65 keys, Nov-2025) and Vindhyavilas (21 keys) opened. Operating EBITDA margin rose from 18% (FY20) to 37% in FY24-25 as room rates outran costs, then slipped to 34.8% in FY26 (flight-catering mix with a higher airport levy, a ₹30 cr political donation, higher repairs and CSR). Attributable profit was ₹739 cr in FY25 and ₹628 cr in FY26; before exceptional items (Mashobra, labour codes) it was ₹768 cr and ₹715 cr.

sections.title: Cash covers capex, dividends and a growing cash pile; returns are good on the old hotels, the new money earns later

blocks.p: EIH turned 97% of FY26 operating EBITDA into operating cash (₹993 cr of ₹1,024 cr). Capex was ₹222 cr in FY24, ₹485 cr in FY25 and ₹696 cr in FY26 (Screener; ₹680 cr on the company's measure, of which ~₹330 cr bought the freehold of the Mumbai hotel land, ~₹125 cr went into Rajgarh and ~₹100 cr into renovations). Dividends are modest: ₹1.50 a share for FY26 (15% of EPS). Surplus funds rose from ₹1,051 cr (Mar-25) to ₹1,335 cr (Mar-26) and ₹1,368 cr (Jun-26). Management guides capex of ₹600-700 cr a year for the next one or two years, rising towards FY29-30 for the bigger projects (Hebbal: two hotels and ~7.6 lakh sq ft of commercial space). blocks.callout: **The capital question:** EIH can fund ₹650-800 cr of capex and its dividend from cash flow and still add to its cash. The question is returns, not money. A new owned luxury hotel takes years to build (Gandikota moved from 2028 to 2030 after a site change; the Grand, shut for renovation, now reopens ~Sep-2028 after unplanned structural and fire-safety work) and ~3 years to stabilise (Rajgarh). sections.title: Earnings quality: real cash and clean debt, but one-offs almost every year and an "EBITDA" that includes other income

bullets: **Exceptional items.** Exceptional items in five of the last six years: FY21 -5, FY22 +41, FY23 -81, FY24 -7, FY25 -39, FY26 -131 (Screener, before tax). FY26: Mashobra and labour codes. FY26 reported attributable profit ₹628 cr vs ₹715 cr before exceptional items (Screener) or ₹812 cr before minorities on the company's own measure. We value and forecast before exceptional items.

**Definitions.** The company's 'EBITDA' includes other income (FY26 Rs1,190 cr vs operating Rs1,024 cr); share of associates (Rs57 cr) is below it. We use operating EBITDA throughout, as Screener and the peers do.
**Political donation.** Rs30 cr donation to a political party in FY26 (AR note 36), booked in other expenses, i.e. inside operating EBITDA (~1 pp of margin).

**Minorities.** Small: ₹29 cr in FY26 (3.9% of profit before minorities), ₹3 cr in Q1FY27; partners hold 40% of Svara Hotels (Amarvilas, Agra), 20% of Oberoi Kerala Hotels and 10-40% of the Indonesian companies.
**Renovations.** Renovation costs are capitalised; the undepreciated value of replaced assets is written off through the P&L (Q1FY27 Rs7.5 cr).
**Cash conversion.** Operating cash 97% of operating EBITDA in FY26 (80% in FY25); company surplus funds up ₹284 cr in FY26 after ₹680 cr of capex and ₹97 cr of dividends.

blocks.callout: **Accounting flag: AMBER.** The cash is real (no bank debt, ~₹1,340 cr net cash, AA+), and nothing in the accounts is aggressive. But exceptional items appear in five of the last six years, the company headlines an EBITDA that includes other income (16% higher than operating EBITDA in FY26), the FY26 profit before exceptional items differs by ₹64 cr between the company and Screener (tax on the Mashobra items), and a ₹30 cr political donation sits inside operating costs.

sections.title: No bank debt, ~₹1,340 cr of net cash after leases, CARE AA+: the balance sheet is not the issue

blocks.p: EIH repaid its last bank loans in FY24 (bank borrowings ₹571 cr at Mar-23, nil since; AR ten-year table). At Mar-2026 the only debt was ₹252 cr of lease liabilities. Cash and bank balances were ₹934 cr and investments ₹656 cr (including the 36.81% stake in listed EIH Associated Hotels at ₹240 cr of book value and the Avis India, Oberoi Mauritius and La Roseraie stakes), so **net cash after leases was ~₹1,338 cr** on Screener's figures, close to the company's "surplus funds" of ₹1,335 cr (₹1,368 cr at Jun-2026). Minority interest is small (₹147 cr). CARE assigned an AA+ (Stable) issuer rating in Dec-2025 and expects capex to be funded from cash and accruals with no debt. The Mashobra settlement removed a ₹91 cr user-fee provision and a ₹136 cr receivable from Mashobra Resort (half of it written off) from the balance sheet in FY26.

blocks.p: EIH is one of the least-covered large hotel stocks in India. The only standing view we could date on or before 30-Sep-2026 is **Axis Capital's initiation (29-Sep-26): Buy, target ₹385** (~30% above the ₹295 close of 28-Sep), arguing that EIH owns marquee assets, its pipeline is reviving, its RevPAR beats peers and its valuation is at a 12-year low, so "a re-rating is due". Earlier coverage (ICICI Securities and ICICI Direct, 2020-23) valued EIH on **EV/EBITDA two years forward** (19-20x FY24E-FY25E in 2023). On our numbers Axis's ₹385 implies ~16.2x Sep-28E EBITDA.

blocks.p: Hotel companies in India are valued on **EV/EBITDA** (enterprise value ÷ operating profit before depreciation): the published IHCL and ITC Hotels reports and every broker that disclosed a method for them use FY28E or Jun-28E EBITDA, and EIH's own coverage used two-year-forward EV/EBITDA. We use the same method on Sep-28E EBITDA (½ FY28E + ½ FY29E, the 12-month-forward year the market will look at in September 2027), in a sum of the parts that deducts minorities, adds the listed associate at market value less 20% and adds net cash, as for IHCL.

The hotels (incl. flight catering) are valued on 100% of Sep-28E operating EBITDA (₹1,400 cr), with lease liabilities in net cash. Minorities took ~4% of profit before minorities in FY25-26, so we deduct 4% of the hotel EV (₹12 a share). EIH Associated Hotels (36.81%, listed) is at its 30-Sep-2026 market value (₹667 cr) less 20%, replacing its ₹240 cr book value in the model's cash; the other JVs (Avis India, Oberoi Mauritius, La Roseraie) stay at book. Net cash is the model's Sep-28E figure (cash and investments less lease liabilities).

blocks.p: House rule: start from the stock's own one-year-forward EV/EBITDA, adjust for how far the sector had moved against its own history by 30-Sep-2026, then test growth, peers, returns and the street. (1) **Window.** EIH's EBITDA broke from Covid losses (FY21 −₹354 cr, FY22 −₹34 cr) to ₹599 cr in FY23; on realised forward EBITDA the 2021-22 multiples look artificially low because the market could not see the rebound, so the turnaround rule starts the window at the break (1-Apr-2022), as for IHCL, and measures the peers' move over the same window; the since-2021 median is a sensitivity. (2) **EV includes minorities**, because the SOTP values 100% of EBITDA and then deducts them (gross-up ~4-6%); without it the median is 15.2x. (3) **Peers.** Three usable peers remain (IHCL, ITC Hotels, Lemon Tree), the minimum, so the set is not widened: Chalet is out (residential flat sales in its trailing EBITDA) and ITC Hotels is measured over the window it has (since 1-Apr-25, listing months skipped). Subsets are sensitivity rows.

sections.title: Our honest summary: a superb hotel company at a fair price for a business that cannot grow its rooms for three years

blocks.callout: **What you are buying:** the finest hotels in India (Oberoi RevPAR ~1.9x the luxury segment), owned-hotel occupancy ~77%, no bank debt and ~₹1,340 cr of net cash, Reliance and ITC on the register, and a pipeline that would add ~20% more owned keys from FY29. Earnings should grow ~14% a year on rates alone.

**What you are paying:** 14.1x one-year-forward EV/EBITDA (its own post-Covid median is 15.9x) and 20.3x our FY28E EPS, while its listed peers trade ~20% below their own medians. On the street's method with our inputs and the house rule for the multiple, the target is {{dcf.tp|inr}} ({{dcf.upside|chg}}): a HOLD. Without the sector adjustment the same SOTP gives ~₹380, close to Axis Capital's ₹385 (a BUY on the rule), so the rating rests on the sector move.
